nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. Then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ equals the $N$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, that is, the result of applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $N$ times to $\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.
nodes.title: The attractor stabilizes after as many stages as there are positions

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on $n$ positions, $p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $T$, $U$ sets of positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set obtained from $\emptyset$ by applying $n$ times the map $X \mapsto (T \cap U) \cup \mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$, where $\mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$ is the controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$.
nodes.title: Attractor inside a set of positions

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. The $n$-th attractor stage $S_n$ of $T$ for $p$ is the set obtained by applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $n$ times to $\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$; thus $S_0 = \emptyset$ and $S_{n+1} = T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$.
nodes.title: Attractor stages

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor operator of $T$ for $p$ is the monotone map on sets of positions sending $X$ to $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.
nodes.title: Attractor operator

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions, $n$ a natural number and $S_n$ the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$. If a position $v$ owned by $p$ lies in the controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$ of $S_n$ for $p$, then the successor that the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ chooses at $v$ lies in $S_n$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy moves into the stage from its controllable predecessor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < N$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from the attractor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < n$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from an attractor stage

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ is the positional strategy of $p$ that at a position $v$ moves to a successor of $v$ lying in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, for the least $n$ for which $v$ has such a successor, and to an arbitrary successor of $v$ if no successor of $v$ lies in any attractor stage.
nodes.title: Attractor strategy

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a set $X$ of positions satisfies $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X) \subseteq X$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$, then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is contained in $X$.
nodes.title: The attractor lies in every closed set

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ is the least fixed point of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ on sets of positions, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.
nodes.title: Attractor

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ in a parity game. An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ (not necessarily a play) conforms to $\sigma$ if $\pi_{i+1} = \sigma(\pi_i)$ for every $i$ such that $p$ owns $\pi_i$.
nodes.title: Plays conforming to a strategy

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, $p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $U$, $X$ sets of positions. The controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set of positions $v \in U$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move of $G$ goes from $v$ to a position of $U \cap X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move of $G$ from $v$ to a position of $U$ ends in $X$.
nodes.title: Controllable predecessor inside a set of positions

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $X$ a set of positions. The controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ of $X$ for $p$ is the set of positions $v$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move from $v$ leads into $X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move from $v$ leads into $X$.
nodes.title: Controllable predecessor

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ and is disjoint from $T$, then $U$ is disjoint from the attractor of $T$ for $p$.
nodes.title: Traps disjoint from a set avoid its attractor

nodes.summary: In a parity game, for every player $p$, no position lies both in the winning region of $p$ and in the winning region of the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: The winning regions of the two players are disjoint

nodes.summary: The dual of an encoded parity game $G$ is the encoded parity game with the same positions and moves in which every position is owned by the other player than in $G$ and has priority one more than in $G$.
nodes.title: Dual parity game

nodes.summary: An encoded finite parity game on the $n$ positions $0, \dots, n - 1$ consists of an owner for each position, given as a Boolean (false for the even player, true for the odd player), a move relation, given as a Boolean-valued $n \times n$ matrix, and a priority for each position, given as a natural number.
nodes.title: Encoded parity game

nodes.summary: For all players $p$ and $q$ of a parity game, $q = p$ or $q$ is the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: Every player is $p$ or the opponent of $p$

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. From every position $v$ of the attractor of $T$ for $p$, the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ forces a visit to $T$: every play from $v$ conforming to it visits $T$.
nodes.title: The attractor strategy forces a visit

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $\sigma$ a positional strategy of $p$, $T$ a set of positions and $v$ a position. The strategy $\sigma$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$ when every play $\pi$ of $G$ with $\pi_0 = v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ visits $T$, that is, $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: Forcing a visit to a set

nodes.summary: An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ of a parity game is a play if for every $i$ there is a move from $\pi_i$ to $\pi_{i+1}$.
nodes.title: Plays of a parity game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The complement of the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is a trap for $p$.
nodes.title: The complement of an attractor is a trap

nodes.summary: In a parity game $G$, the winning region of a player $p$, the set of positions from which $p$ has a winning positional strategy, is a trap for the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: Winning regions are traps for the opponent

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game and $p$ a player. A set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ when, for every position $v \in U$, every move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ belongs to $p$, and some move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ does not belong to $p$. Thus $p$ cannot force the play out of $U$.
nodes.title: Trap for a player

nodes.summary: Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ in a parity game. The joint successor of a position $v$ is $\sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$, and $\tau(v)$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Joint successor of two strategies

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of positions, the positions of maximal priority in $U$ are the positions $v \in U$ whose priority equals the maximal priority of $G$ on $U$.
nodes.title: Positions of maximal priority

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of positions, the maximal priority on $U$ is the largest priority of $G$ at a position of $U$, or $0$ if $U$ is empty.
nodes.title: Maximal priority on a set of positions

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. A position $v$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$ if and only if some positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.
nodes.title: Characterization of the attractor

nodes.summary: In a parity game, let $v$ be a position in the winning region of player $p$ that is owned by the opponent of $p$. Then every position $w$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ is in the winning region of $p$.
nodes.title: Opponent moves stay in the winning region

nodes.summary: In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$ owned by $p$. Then the successor $\sigma(v)$ chosen by $\sigma$ is in the winning region of $p$.
nodes.title: A winning strategy's move stays in the winning region

nodes.summary: In a parity game, every player has a positional strategy, since every position has a move.
nodes.title: Positional strategies exist

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. If a position $v$ is not in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then no positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.
nodes.title: No strategy forces a visit from outside the attractor

nodes.summary: In a parity game, for every player $p$, no infinite sequence of positions (play or not) is won both by $p$ and by the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: No play is won by both players

nodes.summary: In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$, and let $w$ be a position with a move from $v$ to $w$ such that $w = \sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$. Then $\sigma$ wins from $w$.
nodes.title: Winning strategies keep winning along allowed moves

nodes.summary: The opponent of a player of a parity game is the other player: the opponent of the even player is the odd player, and the opponent of the odd player is the even player.
nodes.title: Opponent

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\sigma$ a positional strategy of $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$. The outcome of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a position $v$ is the infinite sequence of positions $v_0, v_1, v_2, \dots$ with $v_0 = v$ in which $v_{i+1}$ is the successor chosen by $\sigma$ at $v_i$ if $p$ owns $v_i$, and the successor chosen by $\tau$ at $v_i$ otherwise. It is the play…
nodes.title: Outcome of two positional strategies

nodes.summary: A parity game on a type of positions consists of an owner for each position, which is one of the two players, a move relation between positions, where the owner of $v$ may move from $v$ to $w$ when $v$ is related to $w$, and a natural-number priority for each position, such that every position has at least one move (there are no dead ends).
nodes.title: Parity game

nodes.summary: A parity game has exactly two players, the even player and the odd player.
nodes.title: Players of a parity game

nodes.summary: A positional (memoryless) strategy for player `p`: a choice of successor at each position, legal at the positions `p` owns. Its values elsewhere are irrelevant.
nodes.title: Positional strategy in a parity game

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, the compressed game has the same owners and moves as $G$ and gives each position $v$ the priority $2r + (q \bmod 2)$, where $q$ is the priority of $v$ in $G$ and $r$ is the number of distinct priorities occurring in $G$ that are smaller than $q$.
nodes.title: Priority compression

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and positions $v$, $w$, the priority of $v$ is smaller than the priority of $w$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ if and only if it is smaller in $G$.
nodes.title: Priority compression preserves and reflects the order of priorities

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, every priority of the priority-compressed game of $G$ is strictly less than $2n$.
nodes.title: Bound on compressed priorities

nodes.summary: For an encoded parity game $G$ and every position $v$, the priority of $v$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ has the same parity as the priority of $v$ in $G$.
nodes.title: Priority compression preserves parity

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The compressed priority of a natural number $p$ is $2r + (p \bmod 2)$, where $r$ is the rank of $p$ in $G$: the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$.
nodes.title: Compressed priority

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is at most the priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is at most the rank of the priority of $v$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of priority ranks

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. For every position $v$ of $G$, the rank of the priority of $v$ is strictly less than the number of distinct priorities that occur in $G$.
nodes.title: Priority ranks are below the number of priorities

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the rank of the priority of $v$.
nodes.title: Strict monotonicity of priority ranks

nodes.summary: The rank of a priority `p` among the distinct priorities occurring in the game: the number of distinct priorities `q < p` that occur.
nodes.title: Rank of a priority in a parity game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every position has a move to some position. The associated parity game has the same positions, moves and priorities, and a position is owned by the odd player if $G$ assigns it to the odd player and by the even player otherwise; every position has a move by the hypothesis on $G$.
nodes.title: The parity game of a serial encoded game

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $A$ the attractor of $T$ for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play starting at a position outside $A$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for the complement of $A$, then $\pi_i \notin T$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: The trap strategy avoids the target

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a trap for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play with $\pi_0 \in U$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for $U$, then $\pi_i \in U$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.title: The trap strategy stays in the trap

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a set of positions. The trap strategy for $U$ is the positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ that, at each position $v$, moves to some position $w \in U$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ if there is one, and to an arbitrary position reachable from $v$ in one move otherwise.
nodes.title: Trap strategy

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions, and let $A$ be the attractor of $T$ for $p$. Then $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(A) = A$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p(A)$ is the controllable predecessor of $A$ for $p$; that is, $A$ is a fixed point of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$.
nodes.title: The attractor is a fixed point

nodes.summary: The positions from which player `p` has a winning positional strategy.
nodes.title: Winning region of a parity game

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game. A positional strategy $\sigma$ of $p$ wins from a position $v$ when every play starting at $v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ (at every position owned by $p$, the play moves to the successor chosen by $\sigma$) is won by $p$.
nodes.title: Winning strategy from a position

nodes.summary: A player wins an infinite sequence of natural-number priorities when the sequence satisfies that player's parity condition: the even player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is even, and the odd player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is odd.
nodes.title: Parity winning condition of a player

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\pi = (\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots)$ an infinite sequence of positions and $j$ a natural number. Then the sequence $(\pi_j, \pi_{j+1}, \dots)$, obtained by dropping the first $j$ positions of $\pi$, is won by $p$ if and only if $\pi$ is won by $p$.
nodes.title: Winning is prefix independent

nodes.summary: Let $p$ be a player of a parity game in which every position has priority at most $d$, for some natural number $d$. Then every infinite sequence of positions, in particular every play, is won by $p$ or by the opponent of $p$.
nodes.title: Bounded priorities give every play a winner

nodes.summary: Let $G$ be a parity game, write $\Omega(v)$ for the priority of a position $v$, and let $p$ be a player. An infinite sequence $\pi = \pi_0 \pi_1 \pi_2 \dots$ of positions of $G$ is won by $p$ when its priority sequence $\Omega(\pi_0) \Omega(\pi_1) \Omega(\pi_2) \dots$ satisfies the parity condition of $p$: among the priorities occurring infinitely often there is a largest one, and it is even if $p$ is the even…
nodes.title: Winner of a play in a parity game

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
